Compared with the earlier, more negative read, the December 16, 2020 FOMC statement pairs acknowledgement of pandemic-driven downside risks with strong, literature-backed tools that tend to mitigate such shocks at the zero lower bound. The explicit average-inflation-targeting “makeup” approach announced in 2020 (Powell’s Jackson Hole shift) and the commitment to keep rates at 0–0.25% until inflation averages 2% align with Svensson and Woodford’s inflation-forecast targeting arguments about anchoring expectations near target. Clarida’s emphasis on the Taylor principle supports maintaining accommodation until the dual-mandate conditions are met. The Fed’s forward guidance and sizable QE—Treasury purchases of at least $80B/month and agency MBS of at least $40B/month—are consistent with the literature that such policies lower term premia, ease financial conditions, and support aggregate demand and credit intermediation when constrained by the zero lower bound. At the same time, the statement’s recognition that COVID-19 elevates economic policy uncertainty and poses “considerable risks” tempers optimism. Balancing these, the overall sentiment should be only slightly negative—less so than the prior -0.25—given the credible commitment to AIT, forward guidance, and QE documented in the monetary policy literature.
